Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Discuss the pathophysiology of posterior glenohumeral instability and the manner in which it
differs from anterior and multidirectional shoulder instability.
Explain the risk factors for and the epidemiology of posterior shoulder instability to maintain a
high index of suspicion, which often is necessary for a timely diagnosis.
Describe the clinical presentation of posterior shoulder instability based on specific physical
examination maneuvers.
List injuries associated with posterior glenohumeral instability.
Identify and interpret appropriate imaging studies in the workup of posterior glenohumeral
instability.
Review appropriate nonsurgical and surgical treatment options for the management of
posterior glenohumeral instability.

Identify technical aspects used in the surgical management of posterior glenohumeral
instability.
Introduction
The glenohumeral joint is inherently unstable and highly susceptible to subluxation,
dislocation, and recurrent instability.
Anterior instability is more common than posterior instability; however, posterior
glenohumeral instability (PGHI) is likely underdiagnosed.
PGHI is common observed in young, active patients and members of the military.
A high index of suspicion must be maintained, and surgeons should obtain a complete history
and perform a thorough physical examination because patients typically present with little
more than vague shoulder pain.
Accurate diagnosis and appropriate, timely management are critical to prevent poor functional
outcomes (Resource 1).

Introduction
The biomechanics of the glenohumeral joint are most notable for providing the shoulder
with the greatest range of motion of all the large joints in the body. The inherently
incongruent joint relies on a complex interplay between osseous and soft-tissue
structures for static and dynamic stability.1 The shoulder is highly susceptible to
dislocation and instability, with PGHI classically representing as few as 2% to 5% of
shoulder instability. Recently, the notion that PGHI is a rare condition representing a
small fraction of the total burden of shoulder instability has been challenged.2
Orthopaedic surgeons in training must develop a thorough understanding of the
pathophysiology and presentation of PGHI to prevent delayed diagnosis and to provide
timely and appropriate care.
Epidemiology
Classically reported to account for approximately 2% to 5% of shoulder instability

2/18

Likely accounts for a higher percentage of shoulder instability; underdiagnosed because of lack
of well-defined diagnostic criteria and vague clinical presentation
Most commonly observed in males in their twenties and thirties, competitive athletes who
participate in overhead sports, and members of the military

Epidemiology
PGHI is far less common than anterior instability and classically has been reported to
account for as few as 2% to 5% of all shoulder instability. PGHI likely represents a higher
burden of the total cases of shoulder instability but is underreported because of the
absence of well-defined diagnostic criteria and the often vague clinical presentation.3,4
Patients who are most commonly affected by PGHI are males in their twenties and
thirties, competitive athletes who participate in overhead sports, members of the
military, and patients with seizure disorders.5
Pathophysiology
Traumatic injury and/or athletic injury
Traumatic posterior dislocation resulting from seizure, electric shock, encephalitis, ethanol
withdrawal, or electrolyte abnormalities often is missed on initial examination.
Recurrent episodes of microtrauma that occur if the shoulder is in a flexed, adducted, and
internally rotated position (overhead sports, bench pressing, etc.) may lead to PGHI.
Can be subdivided into psychogenic, positional, and muscular instability, with muscular
instability being the most common and typically observed in young, active patients

Pathophysiology
Posterior shoulder instability can occur secondary to a posterior shoulder dislocation
caused by high-energy trauma; substantial injury to the shoulder without prior
dislocation; and/or in a more insidious fashion because of repetitive episodes of
microtrauma, in which no single traumatic episode has occurred.3,4 Three distinct
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:46 PM
AAOS | Posterior Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000624
3/18

subgroups of PGHI have been described: psychogenic, positional, and muscular
instability.4 Psychogenic subluxation, which is observed in patients with psychiatric
conditions, is the least common of the three subtypes and begins as voluntary
glenohumeral joint subluxation that eventually leads to symptomatic and involuntary
instability.4 Positional instability results in subluxation if the shoulder is placed in flexion,
adduction, and internal rotation. Patients with positional instability experience
spontaneous reduction with abduction of the arm, with feelings of instability being more
common reported than pain. Muscular instability, the most common cause of PGHI,
often occurs in young, active, athletic patients and is characterized by posterior shoulder
pain and involuntary posterior subluxation.
Anatomy/Associated Lesions
Soft-Tissue
A tear of the posteroinferior aspect of the capsulolabral complex (reverse Bankart lesion) is
observed in patients with known trauma but also may be degenerative in nature.
An avulsion of the posteroinferior aspect of the labrum (Kim lesion)
Posteroinferior capsule laxity secondary to plastic deformation caused by recurrent
subluxation
Reverse humeral avulsion of the glenohumeral ligaments
Posterior labrocapsular periosteal sleeve avulsion
Bone
Increased glenoid retroversion
Posterior glenoid erosion
Reverse bony Bankart lesion
Increased humeral head retrotorsion
Anterior humeral head defects
Reverse Hill-Sachs lesion
Evaluation and Diagnosis

Physical Examination
Findings of posterior instability often are more subtle than those of anterior instability.
Inspection: usually normal; however, atrophy of the posterior rotator cuff muscles may be
observed.
Range of motion: often normal passive/active range of motion, symmetric to the contralateral
upper extremity
Assess for generalized ligamentous laxity.
Palpation: may have tenderness to palpation at the posterior joint line
May have crepitus with internal rotation
Most patients have normal strength.
Except in rare cases in patients with posterior rotator cuff deficiency or nerve injury with
external rotation weakness
Assess scapulohumeral and scapulothoracic mechanics
Frequently confused with scapular winging6
Provocative tests
Posterior load and shift test
Video 1 shows the posterior load and shift test.
Video 1 Yanke AB, Van Thiel G, LeClere LE, Solomon DJ, Provencher MT: Shoulder: Posterior
Shoulder Instability [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2011.

https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/1589__Videos. Accessed September 3, 2021.
Performed with the patient sitting upright with the arm at the side
The humeral head and the proximal humerus are grasped and compressed into the glenoid
fossa.
Anterior and posterior stress is applied, and the degree of translation is noted.
Grading
1: minimal translation
2: the humeral head translates to the glenoid rim
3: the humeral head translates over the glenoid rim but spontaneously reduces
4: the humeral head dislocates and does not spontaneously reduce
The modified posterior load and shift test is performed with the patient in the supine
position, with the arm in neutral rotation and 40° to 60° of abduction and forward flexion.
The same grading system applies.
Jerk test
Figure 1 shows the jerk test.
Performed with patient sitting upright, with the arm flexed to 90° and internally rotated and
the elbow flexed to 90°
A posterior force is generated by applying an axial load to the humerus by pushing on the
flexed elbow.
In patients with posterior instability, this will cause posterior glenohumeral subluxation or
dislocation.
The arm is then extended. A positive test is noted if the glenohumeral joint reduces with a
painful jerk.

Figure 1 Clinical photographs show the jerk test. A, A posterior force is applied along the axis of
the humerus, with the arm in forward flexion and internal rotation. This will cause the humeral
head to subluxate posteriorly out of the glenoid socket. B, As the arm is brought into extension,
a clunk will be felt as the humerus reduces into the glenoid cavity. (Reproduced from Millett PJ,
Clavert P, Hatch GF III, Warner JJ: Recurrent posterior shoulder instability. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2006;14[8]:464-476.)
Kim test
Performed with patient sitting upright, with the arm abducted 90°
The examiner flexes the shoulder to 45° of forward flexion while applying an axial load on
the elbow and a posteroinferior directed force on proximal humerus.
The test is positive if pain is present.
The Kim test can be performed to identify posteroinferior labral lesions.
Posterior stress test
Performed with the patient in the supine position, with the arm flexed to 90° and internally
rotated (Figure 2)
A posteriorly directed axial load is applied to the humerus while stabilizing the back of the
shoulder.
The test is positive if humeral subluxation or dislocation over posterior glenoid rim is
palpated or observed.
A positive Jerk test and a positive Kim test is 97% sensitive for the diagnosis of a posterior
labral tear.

7/18

Figure 2 Clinical photograph shows the posterior stress test. A posterior force is applied through
the humerus. The test is positive if palpable crepitus or subluxation is noted. Often pain is
elicited; however, this is not as specific a finding. (Reproduced from Millett PJ, Clavert P, Hatch GF
III, Warner JJ: Recurrent posterior shoulder instability. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2006;14[8]:464-476.)

Physical Examination
Physical examination findings of PGHI often are subtle. Many patients have equal
strength and symmetric range of motion.7 The examiner should evaluate for rotator
cuff muscle deficiency, assess shoulder mechanics, and evaluate for generalized
ligamentous laxity.7,8 The posterior load and shift test is performed with the patient
sitting upright with the arm at the side. The humeral head and the proximal humerus
are grasped and compressed to the glenoid fossa. Anterior and posterior stress is
applied, and the degree of translation is noted.7 This test can be modified by
performing it with the patient in the supine position, with the arm in neutral rotation
with 40° to 60° of abduction and forward flexion.
The jerk test is performed with the patient sitting upright with the arm flexed to 90° and
internally rotated and the elbow flexed to 90°. A posterior force is generated by
applying an axial load to the humerus by pushing on the flexed elbow. In patients with
glenohumeral instability, this will cause posterior subluxation or dislocation. A positive
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:46 PM
AAOS | Posterior Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000624
8/18

test is noted if the arm is subsequently extended and the glenohumeral joint reduces
with a painful jerk.7
The Kim test is performed with the patient sitting upright with the arm abducted to 90°.
The examiner flexes the shoulder forward to 45° while applying an axial load on the
elbow and a posteroinferior directed force on the proximal humerus. Pain with this
maneuver indicates a positive test.7 If the Jerk test and the Kim test are positive, the
sensitivity for the diagnosis of a posterior labral tear is 97%.7
The posterior stress test is performed with the patient in the supine position, with the
arm flexed to 90° and internally rotated. A posteriorly directed axial load is applied to
the humerus while stabilizing the shoulder. The test is positive if humeral subluxation or
dislocation over the posterior glenoid rim occurs.7
Hypermobility can be assessed via the Beighton score (Table 1), which is a nine-point
scale of four maneuvers: passive dorsiflexion and hyperextension of the fifth
metacarpophalangeal joint beyond 90°, passive apposition of the thumb to the flexor
aspect of the forearm, passive hyperextension of the elbow beyond 10°, and passive
hyperextension of the knee beyond 10°. Each of these four maneuvers can have a
maximum of two points, one each for right or left. The final maneuver is scored as zero
points or one point for active forward flexion of the trunk with the knees fully extended
so the palms of the hands rest flat on the floor. In addition, the Gagey test assesses the
inferior glenohumeral ligament, with passive abduction greater than 105° considered
abnormal (Resource 2).

Radiographs often are normal.
Dynamic radiographs can confirm the diagnosis in patients with a volitional component.


Imaging Studies
Imaging begins with radiography. Necessary radiographs to obtain in patient with PGHI
include a true AP view in neutral, internal rotation, and external rotation; a trans-
scapular or Y view; and an axillary view.7 Radiographs are necessary to evaluate whether
the glenohumeral joint is reduced, the status of the posterior glenoid rim, and if
impaction fractures of the humeral head are present. In many patients with posterior
shoulder instability, radiographs will be normal. Dynamic radiographs may be beneficial
in patients with a possible volitional component to their symptoms.7 MRI is the best
imaging modality for evaluating injuries or lesions of the capsule and labrum. MRI is
indicated in patients with chronic instability who do not have a history of an acute
traumatic dislocation.7 MRI also is useful in assessing a Kim lesion, which is a concealed
avulsion of the deep posteroinferior labrum with an intact superficial labrum.7 CT is
most helpful in evaluating bony anatomy, including the articular surface. CT best
demonstrates subtle humeral head fractures and glenoid rim abnormalities.7 With the
addition of intra-articular contrast, CT affords excellent visualization of the joint surface.6
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Successful in the most patients (65% to 80%)
Physical therapy aimed at strengthening the dynamic stabilizers of the shoulder to
compensate for deficient static stabilizers
Surgical Management
If nonsurgical management fails, surgical management is warranted.
Considerations regarding pathoanatomy and the appropriate procedure are crucial to
successful outcomes.
If a posterior Bankart lesion is present, perform Bankart repair.
If excessive capsulolabral laxity is present, a posterior capsular shift with or without rotator
interval closure is indicated.

If glenoid erosion is present, bone grafting should be implemented in the area. Glenoid
retroversion can be managed via a posterior opening wedge glenoid osteotomy.
Techniques
Arthroscopic posterior stabilization (Video 2)
Ideal for patients with a posterior Bankart lesion
Position the patient in the lateral decubitus or beach-chair position.
Capsulolabral injury is repaired with the use of suture anchors.
Capsular redundancy is reduced via capsular shift.
Open posteroinferior capsular shift
Position the patient in the lateral decubitus or beach-chair position.
The incision is made in the posterior axillary fold.
The deltoid is split in line with its fibers to expose the infraspinatus and the teres minor.
The infraspinatus is split to expose the capsule.
The infraspinatus tendon raphe identified and split along direction of the fibers.
Avoid damage to the suprascapular nerve and the teres minor by not dividing the muscle
more than 1.5 cm medial to the glenoid.
The neurovascular interval between the infraspinatus and the teres minor also may be
used. Although a safe dissection plane, it may be difficult to define and exposes the
glenoid near its inferior margin.
A capsulotomy is performed via a horizontal incision from medial to lateral; however, it may
be a T-shaped or laterally based capsulotomy.
The capsulolabral sleeve is elevated off the posteroinferior glenoid.
Any posterior labral injury is repaired with the use of absorbable sutures.
Suture anchors are placed along the posterior glenoid rim.
The capsule is repaired with the arm in 20° of abduction and neutral rotation.
Posterior bone graft
Useful in patients with an acquired bony defect of the posterior glenoid
Can be intra-articular or extra-articular, with capsular advancement anterior and medial to
the graft to serve as soft-tissue interposition
Avoid excessive medial placement (ineffective buttressing) or lateral placement (humeral
impingement).
The preferred bone graft source is the inner table of the iliac crest.
Opening wedge glenoid osteotomy
Indicated in patients with glenoid retroversion greater than 20°
Similar patient positioning and exposure as that for open capsular shift

An osteotomy is performed approximately 10 mm medial and parallel to the joint line.
The anterior cortex is preserved.
Autologous tricortical bone graft is used to fill the void and is press fit or secured with the
use of a screw.
Derotational humeral osteotomy
Indicated in patients with more chronic instability
Deltopectoral approach; may require tenotomy of the pectoralis major from anterior lip of
the bicipital groove and the latissimus dorsi with repair.
Osteotomy of the humeral head at the surgical neck and derotation with plate and screw
fixation


Management
Nonsurgical management typically is the first line of treatment for patients with PGHI
and is successful in most patients (65% to 80%).7 The mainstay of nonsurgical
management is physical therapy aimed at strengthening the dynamic stabilizers of the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:46 PM
AAOS | Posterior Shoulder Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000624
15/18

shoulder.7 If nonsurgical management fails, the pathoanatomy must be thoroughly
evaluated to successfully correct the underlying issue. If a posterior Bankart lesion is
present, Bankart repair must be performed (Video 3). Excessive capsulolabral laxity can
be managed via a posterior capsular shift with or without rotator interval closure. If
glenoid erosion is present, bone grafting should be implemented in the area. Glenoid
retroversion can be managed via a posterior opening wedge glenoid osteotomy.7

[video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020.
https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/21633__Videos. Accessed November 3,
2022.
